\textit{Remark.} Proposition~2 assumes binary episode rewards for analytical tractability. Under non-binary rewards (e.g., with per-step penalties for invalid actions), the group mean $\mu$ is nonzero even when all episodes fail, but the qualitative conclusion is preserved: advantage sign is determined by relative episode performance within the group, not by local action quality within individual windows. Section~\ref{sec:sign_verification} validates this empirically using the full reward structure.

\textit{Penalty reward effect on credit agreement.} Proposition~2 predicts 19.1\% correct-sign rate (i.e., 80.9\% incorrect) under pure binary reward. Our experiments include a $-0.1$ penalty per invalid action, making the reward non-binary. This penalty introduces variance within failed episodes: windows with valid actions receive $R_k = 0$ while windows with invalid actions receive $R_k = -0.1h$. Within a failed episode, the penalty-induced variance can occasionally produce positive $\hat{A}_k$ for windows with valid actions even when $\mu > 0$, since the normalization accounts for intra-group variance. This shifts the empirical credit agreement from the theoretical 19.1\% toward 52\%---still marginally above the 50\% random baseline ($p{=}0.025$; $+$2pp effect size) and far below the level needed for convergence. A binomial test formally rejects $H_0{:}\, P = 0.191$ ($z = 45.9$, $p < 10^{-100}$), confirming that the gap between 19.1\% (binary theory) and 52\% (penalty-reward measurement) reflects the reward structure difference, not a failure of the theoretical framework.
tool_args.new_string:
\textit{Two calibers of credit assignment failure.} Proposition~2 and the empirical credit agreement rate (Section~\ref{sec:sign_verification}) quantify different aspects of credit assignment failure under different reward structures; both confirm that advantage sign carries insufficient information about local action quality.

\textit{Binary caliber} ($P(\text{correct} \mid \text{update}) \leq 19.1\%$). Under pure binary reward $R \in \{0, r_+\}$, the GRPO advantage $\hat{A}_k = R_k - \bar{R}_g$ has its sign entirely determined by episode outcome: all windows in a successful episode receive positive advantage, all windows in a failed episode receive negative advantage whenever the group contains at least one success. This deterministic sign-episode mapping---confirmed empirically at 100\% ($n{=}157$; Section~\ref{sec:sign_verification})---means Proposition~2's upper bound applies directly: at most 19.1\% of non-zero gradient updates carry the correct sign.

\textit{Penalty caliber} (credit agreement $= 52.1\%$). Introducing a format penalty $r_- = -0.1$ per invalid action breaks this deterministic mapping. Within a failed episode, windows with valid actions receive $R_k = 0$ while windows with invalid actions receive $R_k = -0.1h$. This intra-episode variance shifts $\bar{R}_g$ downward, allowing some valid-action windows in failed episodes to obtain $\hat{A}_k > 0$ despite overall failure. Credit agreement rises from 19.1\% to 52.1\%---but this is marginally above random chance (Cohen's $h = 0.041$, below the 0.2 small-effect threshold), carrying negligible information about local action quality.

\textit{Complementary evidence.} The two calibers capture qualitatively different failure modes: 19.1\% reflects deterministic misattribution (advantage sign systematically tracks the wrong signal), while 52.1\% reflects near-random noise (advantage sign carries almost no local information). Both are far below the level required for policy improvement. The gap between them is itself informative: it quantifies how penalty-induced variance transforms the failure mode from systematic wrong-sign to random noise, without repairing credit assignment. A binomial test rejects $H_0{:}\, P = 0.191$ ($z = 45.9$, $p < 10^{-100}$), formally confirming that the two calibers measure different quantities.
